title: Improve limit -1 performance
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Noticed that limit -1 can be quite slow, specially while ingesting data on a large table.

This can be tested on demo box with the new dataset.

```
select * from market_data limit -1;
select * from market_data latest by symbol;
```
Explain says latest on does a frame backward scan, while limit -1 needs to skip over billions of frames, then do a row forward scan.

```
Limit lo: -1 skip-over-rows: 154330575 limit: 1
    PageFrame
        Row forward scan
        Frame forward scan on: core_price
```
or for a larger table
```
Limit lo: -1 skip-over-rows: 1744670104 limit: 1
    PageFrame
        Row forward scan
        Frame forward scan on: market_data
```
I’ve observed during heavy ingestion latest on is way faster (few ms) than limit -1 (several seconds)

Equivalent plans for the latest on
```
LatestByDeferredListValuesFiltered
    Frame backward scan on: core_price
```
```
LatestByDeferredListValuesFiltered
    Frame backward scan on: market_data
```

As hinted by @participant5, I tried

```
select * from market_data order by timestamp desc limit 1;
```

And this was good, just a few milliseconds. With this plan

```
Limit lo: 1 skip-over-rows: 0 limit: 1
    PageFrame
        Row backward scan
        Frame backward scan on: market_data
```

### Describe the solution you'd like.

I would expect `limit -1` to apply the same frame backward strategy that the `order by desc limit 1` is doing

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
@reporter 
It would be great if LIMIT -1 could leverage the same frame backward scan strategy used by ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1. This would significantly improve performance for queries aiming to fetch the most recent row(s), especially under heavy ingestion workloads.

`SELECT * FROM market_data ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1;`

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
This is a little tricky. Things to consider:
- skipping over N rows on plain table should be quick enough, it does not involve iterating over the number of rows reported in the plan. May be we can look into improving performance of that?
- the workaround `SELECT * FROM market_data ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1;` works only for `-1` case specifically, for `-2` or less the order of the rows will be different compared to the original query.
- more accurate workaround would be `(select * from trades order by timestamp desc limit 1) order by timestamp;`. However this is not 100% equivalent. For rows with identical timestamp the order or the rows will be different to the order rows were stored in the database
- on balance, this is a non-trivial change

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
indeed, just checked - this is a complex problem, requires a mild redesign and intrinsic knowledge of the query execution system. Definitely not good as new issues.

What indeed happens is that "skipRows()" in `PageFrameRecordCursorImpl` is quite heavy, it opens partitions even those that need not to be opened (skipped). Reworking the logic to align to the above workarounds will lead to incorrect results.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
> for -2 or less the order of the rows will be different compared to the original query.

That's trivial to fix by an outer ORDER BY.

As for page frame init / mmap, we could make it lazy. The entry point is `PageFrameMemoryPool#navigateTo()`.
